hero.role_start: I like finding out why things work —
hero.tagline: Freshman · St. Charles North High School · Class of 2030
hero.intro: In sixth grade, I built a LEGO grabber that could reach and grip, but couldn't bend the way I wanted. That question stayed with me. Today, I'm building robots and exploring engineering questions about life in space. This is where I share what I build, what goes wrong, and what I learn along the way.

projects.label: AERO-LITE · SPACE SYSTEMS
projects.award_note: Top Individual Award · Middle School Division · NASA Carbon Capture Challenge 2026
projects.headline: How could astronauts manage CO₂ on the Moon?
projects.description: I started AERO-LITE after learning about a carbon capture challenge at Space Center Houston. My first approach was to compress cabin air directly, but after examining the problem more closely, I redesigned the system to concentrate CO₂ first. That decision shaped the prototype I eventually built.

projects.image_caption: Phase 1 prototype: three mason jars, a live ESP32-S3, and a dashboard updating every second.

projects.label: ASHTAVAKRA · ROBOTICS
projects.note: Independent project · Started in 8th grade, still evolving in high school
projects.headline: The LEGO question became a Wi-Fi-controlled robotic arm.
projects.description: After learning Arduino, electronics, and programming, I returned to that early idea as a six-degree-of-freedom arm controlled through a browser. I wrote the Arduino firmware myself, connected eight servos through a motor driver, and built the browser controls — so a command on screen could move a real joint.

build_log.heading: Build Log
build_log.intro: What worked. What did not. What I learned.

cards.headline: The Robotic Arm Didn't Work. So I Stopped Guessing.
cards.excerpt: I started by changing code until something worked. After a fried board, a missing I2C device, and strange servo channels, I learned a better way to solve: isolate one problem, test one assumption, and collect evidence before changing anything.

cards.headline: The Calculation That Changed My Design
cards.excerpt: I wanted to compress cabin air directly, but compression alone would not separate out CO₂. The numbers made me rethink the design: capture CO₂ first, then consider compressing a concentrated stream. That is where AERO-LITE changed direction.

cards.headline: Building It Wasn't the Same as Explaining It
cards.excerpt: Eight slides and a prototype with live CO₂ readings. What I learned about explaining a technical project without exaggerating what my first prototype actually proved.

beyond.heading: Beyond the Workbench
beyond.note: A little about the person behind the projects.
beyond.quote: The projects may be mine, but the curiosity behind them has never grown alone.
paragraphs: My dad gave me my first Arduino kit as a birthday gift. That small box of parts opened a new way to learn: ask a question, try something, and talk through what happened.
He still mentors me with feedback and encouragement. That support has helped me keep investigating, revise my thinking, and explain what I am learning in my own voice.

how_i_build.heading: How I Build
how_i_build.note: The tools matter. The way I test, debug, and document matters more.

groups.title: Build

groups.title: Code

about.page_subtitle: What I am building now, what shaped it, and what I learned along the way.
about.intro: The projects on this page look very different, but they all started the same way: I found something I did not understand and wanted to figure it out. Whether it was making an LED blink, building a robotic arm, or researching how astronauts could manage CO₂ on the Moon, each challenge pulled me toward the next one.

timeline.title: From Control to Vision
paragraphs: I started high school with a challenging course load that matches where I want to go: PLTW Principles of Engineering Honors, Algebra 2 Honors, Biology Honors, English Honors, and AP World History. I wanted freshman year to push me both technically and academically while I continued building projects outside the classroom.

sections.heading: Summer 2026: A Working Ashtavakra
sections.text: I turned Ashtavakra from an early test into a working 3D-printed robotic arm that I can control over Wi-Fi. It can move the way I tell it to, but it still depends on me for almost every decision.

sections.heading: Fall 2026: Giving It Vision
sections.text: I am now working on the Vision AI part of Ashtavakra. My goal is for the arm to recognize objects and eventually use what it sees to help decide how to move. It is still a work in progress, and I am learning a lot while trying to make the different parts work together.

timeline.title: Building With Purpose
paragraphs: In 8th grade, I started thinking differently about my projects. Instead of only asking, "Can I build this?" I started asking, "What problem could this solve?"

sections.heading: Fall 2025: Ashtavakra Begins
sections.text: The idea came from a LEGO grabber I had built years earlier. I started Ashtavakra as my own robotic-arm project and built an early version to see if I could get the mechanics, electronics, and code working together.

sections.heading: Spring 2026: AERO-LITE
sections.text: I entered Space Center Houston's Carbon Capture Challenge and built AERO-LITE, a project focused on removing CO₂ from the air in a future lunar habitat. I had to learn about chemistry, sensors, electronics, programming, and a lot of things I had never worked with before.

sections.heading: May 2026: Top Individual Award
sections.text: AERO-LITE received the Top Individual Award in the Middle School division. I was excited about winning, but what mattered even more was realizing that I could start with something I barely understood, keep learning, and turn the idea into a working project.

timeline.title: Trying More on My Own
paragraphs: I started building projects that combined code, sensors, and movement. An Arduino car taught me how to work with motors and sensors, and later I discovered the ESP32 and built a simple web page that let me control servos from my phone.

This was also when I started moving away from copying tutorials and trying more ideas of my own. By the end of 7th grade, I signed up for PLTW Introduction to Engineering because I wanted to learn more before taking on bigger projects.

timeline.title: The Spark
paragraphs: My dad gave me an Arduino Starter Kit for my birthday. I started with a blinking LED, then buttons, sensors, and projects I found online. Most of them did not work the first time, but I loved seeing a few lines of code make something happen in the real world.

timeline.title: Gears Before Code
paragraphs: I spent a lot of time building LEGO and other mechanical sets with motors, gears, and moving parts. I liked following the instructions at first, but I liked taking things apart and changing them even more.
By the end of 5th grade, I wanted to do more than connect gears and motors. I wanted to control what I built with code.

timeline.title: Looking Ahead
paragraphs: Ashtavakra: After finishing the Vision AI work, I want to keep exploring how the arm can do simple tasks with less help from me.
AERO-LITE: I want to continue testing the project and collect better data to understand how well the CO₂ capture idea actually works.
Aerospace: I want to take on bigger aerospace and rocketry projects that push me to learn more physics, engineering, teamwork, and testing.

Keep Building: As I learn more math, science, programming, and engineering, I want my projects to grow with me. I hope I keep choosing things that are just a little beyond what I already know how to do.

beliefs.title: Start Small
beliefs.text: Big projects feel less overwhelming when I start with one simple goal. Make one motor move. Read one sensor. Get one part working. Then build from there.

beliefs.title: Test, Don't Guess
beliefs.text: When something does not work, I try to change one thing at a time and see what actually happens. I have learned that guessing usually creates more problems.

beliefs.title: Learn From What Breaks
beliefs.text: I have burned boards, wired things incorrectly, and spent hours chasing the wrong problem. Those mistakes are frustrating, but they are also the parts I usually remember and learn from the most.

beliefs.title: Keep It Simple
beliefs.text: I used to think adding more parts and features made a project better. Now I try to find the simplest solution that does the job well before making it more complicated.

beliefs.title: Build Safely
beliefs.text: Working with batteries, motors, heat, and moving parts has taught me to think about what could go wrong before I turn something on. A working project is not worth much if it is not safe.

beliefs.title: Share What I Learn
beliefs.text: I document my projects because I know how helpful it is to find someone else's explanation when I am stuck. If my notes help another student get past a problem, they are worth writing.

aero_lite.title: AERO-LITE
aero_lite.subtitle: A regenerative CO₂ preprocessor for lunar habitats. Started mid-March 2026 after an email from Space Center Houston. Built by an 8th grader.
aero_lite.prototype_image_alt: AERO-LITE Phase 1 prototype — three mason jars with zeolite beads, silica gel, and CO₂ sensors on a desk

problem_cards.title: ISS Solution: CDRA
problem_cards.fatal: Does not work on the Moon — no 'into space.'

problem_cards.title: AERO-LITE
lines: Early prototype: zeolite, silica gel, sensors, and dashboard.
problem_cards.win: Goal: capture, release, and reuse the sorbent. Full-cycle performance still needs testing.

stages.title: DRY
stages.text: Silica gel strips moisture from cabin air. Humidity kills CO₂ capture efficiency, so this happens first.

stages.title: TRAP
stages.text: Zeolite 13X bed captures CO₂ at room temperature. Nitrogen and oxygen pass through. Clean air returns to the cabin.

stages.title: RELEASE
stages.text: Planned regeneration stage: use controlled heating to release CO₂ adsorbed on the zeolite. The first prototype simulated heater control; repeatable regeneration and resulting CO₂ concentration still need to be tested.

stages.title: COMPRESS
stages.text: Planned downstream stage: compress a CO₂-rich stream into a buffer tank for possible use with a Sabatier system. The compressor, pressure target, and continuous-feed integration require future validation.

aero_lite.cycle_note: Intended control schedule: ADSORB (~5 min) → REGEN (~1 min) → PURGE (~15 sec), totaling ~6 min 15 sec. This is a design setting, not a validated full regeneration-cycle measurement. The proposed buffer tank is intended to smooth the intermittent output for downstream use; that integration remains to be tested.
aero_lite.prototype_text: This is not a rendering. It is three mason jars on my desk, a live ESP32-S3, and a web dashboard that updates every second.
prototype_bullets: Stage 1: Silica gel beads (orange, indicating type)
Stage 2+3: Zeolite 13X pellets in a shared bed
Stage 4: CO₂ buffer tank with pressure sensor
Control: ESP32-S3 DevKitC-1 with TCA9548A multiplexer
Dashboard: Pure HTML/CSS/JS, polling JSON API at 1 Hz
aero_lite.prototype_data: One recorded dashboard snapshot: Cabin sensor 1,029 ppm; Purified sensor 477 ppm. These readings illustrate the prototype sensor output, not validated CO₂ capture efficiency or sustained performance.

learnings.title: 💡 Capture First, Compress Later
learnings.text: I initially thought compressing cabin air could give me a useful CO₂ stream. Then I realized compression alone does not separate the gases. I redesigned the concept to capture CO₂ before any downstream compression. Actual power and mass savings still need testing.

learnings.title: 🔥 Thermal Swing > Pressure Swing
learnings.text: Pressure swing uses less energy, but vacuum seals in microgravity are catastrophic leak risks. A PTC heater with a bimetallic cutoff is safer — even if the ESP32 crashes.

learnings.title: 📊 The Dashboard Is Evidence, Not an Efficiency Test
learnings.text: Real hardware and live sensor readings made the project concrete. One dashboard snapshot did not establish capture efficiency; I need repeatable experiments and controlled measurements for that.

aero_lite.repo_text: All firmware, schematics, 3D models, and documentation are open source.

ashtavakra.title: Ashtavakra Robotic Arm
ashtavakra.subtitle: A Wi-Fi-controlled 6-DoF robotic arm with custom firmware and a browser-based controller. Started in 8th grade and still evolving in high school.
ashtavakra.prototype_image_alt: Ashtavakra robotic arm with multiple servo-driven joints and gripper

problem_cards.title: More Than a Kit
lines: Most robotic-arm kits already include the control system.
That makes them easy to assemble, but harder to learn from.
problem_cards.fatal: I wanted to understand what happens between a control on a screen and a joint moving.

problem_cards.title: Movement Was Not Enough
lines: Servos could move, but motion was jerky.
Physical alignment and channel mapping were inconsistent.
problem_cards.fatal: A robot that moves is not automatically a robot that moves well.

problem_cards.title: My Approach
problem_cards.win: Build the control system myself, test it, break it, understand it, and improve it.

stages.title: CONTROL
stages.text: A phone or laptop opens the web controller I built using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

stages.title: PROCESS
stages.text: Commands travel over Wi-Fi to an Arduino UNO R4 WiFi running my motion-control firmware.

stages.title: DRIVE
stages.text: The Arduino communicates over I2C with an Emakefun Motor Driver V5.2, which controls all eight servos.

stages.title: MOVE
stages.text: The servos move the base, arm, wrist, and gripper while the firmware handles calibration, speed, and smooth motion.

ashtavakra.cycle_note: The control path is simple: Browser → Wi-Fi → Arduino UNO R4 WiFi → I2C Motor Driver → Servos → Robotic Arm.
ashtavakra.prototype_text: Ashtavakra is not controlled by a pre-built robotics app. I wrote the Arduino firmware and browser interface, mapped the servo channels, calibrated the joints, and added the tools I needed as problems appeared.
prototype_bullets: Servo driver: Emakefun Motor Driver V5.2 at I2C address 0x60
Motion: 6-DoF arm + gripper with 7 user controls and 1 twin support servo
Firmware: C++ with servo offsets, speed control, S-curve motion, reset, and emergency stop
ashtavakra.prototype_data: Current result: a working robotic arm that can be controlled wirelessly from a phone or laptop without installing a dedicated app.

learnings.title: 🔍 Test Instead of Guess
learnings.text: When the motor driver would not respond, I stopped changing the main program and wrote a small I2C scanner. It found the board at 0x60. That changed how I debug problems: isolate one assumption, test it, then move on.

learnings.title: ⚙️ Software Can Fix Physical Problems
learnings.text: Some servo horns were slightly misaligned. Instead of repeatedly rebuilding the joints, I added software offsets so each servo could be calibrated individually.

learnings.title: 🧩 Build the Whole System
learnings.text: The hardest part was not making one servo move. It was getting mechanics, electronics, firmware, Wi-Fi, and the browser interface to work together reliably.

ashtavakra.repo_text: Firmware, web controller, architecture, design decisions, and project documentation are available in the public repository.

blog.page_subtitle: Build logs, debugging stories, and things I wish someone told me earlier. I write these because the gap between 'I want to build that' and 'I actually built that' is filled with mistakes most people never talk about.
